findings.title: Live Host Discovered
findings.remediation_brief: Reconcile all discovered hosts against the authorised asset inventory and investigate any unexpected or unregistered hosts.
findings.description: A host was confirmed active on the network by responding to one or more probe types (ICMP, TCP SYN, ARP, or UDP), expanding the known attack surface.
findings._x_remediation: Reconcile all discovered hosts against the authorised asset inventory and investigate any unexpected or unregistered hosts.

findings.title: Open Port Discovered
findings.remediation_brief: Inventory all open ports against expected service requirements; close or restrict access to ports that serve no legitimate business purpose via host-based or network firewall rules.
findings.description: A TCP or UDP port was confirmed open on the target host, indicating an exposed service that contributes to the overall network attack surface.
findings._x_remediation: Inventory all open ports against expected service requirements; close or restrict access to ports that serve no legitimate business purpose via host-based or network firewall rules.

findings.title: Service Version Identified
findings.remediation_brief: Suppress version information where possible. Keep all identified services up to date.
findings.description: A specific software version was identified from a service banner or nmap version detection. This information can be cross-referenced against CVE databases to identify known vulnerabilities.
findings._x_remediation: Suppress version information where possible. Keep all identified services up to date.

findings.title: DHCP Lease Assigned to Device
findings.remediation_brief: No action required; informational record.
findings.description: The device successfully obtained a DHCP lease from the gearbox DHCP server. The assigned IP address and MAC address are documented for the assessment.
findings._x_remediation: No action required; informational record.

findings.title: LLMNR/NBT-NS Broadcast Poisoning Possible
findings.remediation_brief: Disable LLMNR and NetBIOS-NS via Group Policy (Network > DNS Client) and enforce DNS-only name resolution across all hosts.
findings.description: LLMNR and/or NBT-NS broadcast name resolution is active on the network, allowing an attacker to poison responses with Responder and capture NTLMv1/v2 hashes for offline cracking or relay.
findings._x_remediation: Disable LLMNR and NetBIOS-NS via Group Policy (Network > DNS Client) and enforce DNS-only name resolution across all hosts.

findings.title: LLMNR/NBT-NS Broadcast Poisoning Possible
findings.remediation_brief: Disable LLMNR and NetBIOS-NS via Group Policy (Network > DNS Client) and enforce DNS-only name resolution across all hosts.
findings.description: LLMNR and/or NBT-NS broadcast name resolution is active on the network, allowing an attacker to poison responses with Responder and capture NTLMv1/v2 hashes for offline cracking or relay.
findings._x_remediation: Disable LLMNR and NetBIOS-NS via Group Policy (Network > DNS Client) and enforce DNS-only name resolution across all hosts.

findings.title: NTLM Hash Captured via Responder
findings.remediation_brief: Disable LLMNR and NBT-NS as described in GB-DISC-005/006. Enforce SMB signing. Implement network segmentation. Use strong, unique passwords resistant to offline cracking.
findings.description: Responder successfully captured an NTLMv1 or NTLMv2 challenge-response hash in response to a poisoned LLMNR/NBT-NS reply. The captured hash can be subjected to offline dictionary or brute-force cracking or used directly in NTLM relay attacks.
findings._x_remediation: Disable LLMNR and NBT-NS as described in GB-DISC-005/006. Enforce SMB signing. Implement network segmentation. Use strong, unique passwords resistant to offline cracking.

findings.title: Cleartext Credentials in Traffic Capture
findings.remediation_brief: Replace all cleartext authentication protocols with encrypted equivalents. Use TLS for web, SSH for remote management, SNMPv3 for SNMP.
findings.description: Cleartext credentials (username/password) were observed in captured network traffic. The device transmitted authentication information over an unencrypted protocol (e.g., HTTP Basic Auth, FTP, Telnet, SNMP v1/v2c).
findings._x_remediation: Replace all cleartext authentication protocols with encrypted equivalents. Use TLS for web, SSH for remote management, SNMPv3 for SNMP.

findings.title: Weak or Default Credentials Accepted
findings.remediation_brief: Replace all default credentials with strong, unique secrets and enforce a password policy prior to any deployment.
findings.description: The target accepted well-known default or factory-set credentials, granting unauthorised access.
findings._x_remediation: Replace all default credentials with strong, unique secrets and enforce a password policy prior to any deployment.

findings.title: Nessus Critical Vulnerability
findings.remediation_brief: Apply vendor patch immediately. If no patch is available, implement network isolation and document as an accepted risk with a defined remediation timeline.
findings.description: Nessus Professional identified a critical severity vulnerability (CVSS ≥ 9.0). This typically represents unauthenticated remote code execution, authentication bypass with full system impact, or a well-known exploit with active weaponisation.
findings._x_remediation: Apply vendor patch immediately. If no patch is available, implement network isolation and document as an accepted risk with a defined remediation timeline.

findings.title: Nessus High Vulnerability
findings.remediation_brief: Patch within the defined SLA for high-severity findings. Apply compensating controls if immediate patching is not feasible.
findings.description: Nessus Professional identified a high severity vulnerability (CVSS 7.0–8.9). Often exploitable by local or adjacent attackers with limited prerequisites.
findings._x_remediation: Patch within the defined SLA for high-severity findings. Apply compensating controls if immediate patching is not feasible.

findings.title: Nessus Medium Vulnerability
findings.remediation_brief: Schedule remediation within the standard patch cycle.
findings.description: Nessus Professional identified a medium severity vulnerability (CVSS 4.0–6.9). May require special conditions to exploit but presents meaningful risk.
findings._x_remediation: Schedule remediation within the standard patch cycle.

findings.title: Nessus Low / Informational Finding
findings.remediation_brief: Include in routine hardening backlog.
findings.description: Nessus Professional identified a low-severity or informational finding. May represent configuration observations or version disclosures without direct exploitability.
findings._x_remediation: Include in routine hardening backlog.

findings.title: CVE-Matched Service Banner
findings.remediation_brief: Update the affected software to a patched version. Cross-reference the specific CVE for vendor-recommended mitigations.
findings.description: The service banner matched a known CVE in the NVD or OSV.dev database. The software version identified in the banner is listed as affected by a publicly disclosed vulnerability with an available CVSS score.
findings._x_remediation: Update the affected software to a patched version. Cross-reference the specific CVE for vendor-recommended mitigations.

findings.title: End-of-Life Software Detected
findings.remediation_brief: Upgrade to a supported version. If upgrade is constrained, apply network isolation and create a formal remediation plan.
findings.description: A service banner or version string indicates software that has passed its vendor end-of-life date. No further security patches will be issued, and any future vulnerabilities will be permanently unaddressed.
findings._x_remediation: Upgrade to a supported version. If upgrade is constrained, apply network isolation and create a formal remediation plan.

findings.title: End-of-Life Operating System Detected
findings.remediation_brief: Upgrade to a supported OS version. If the device cannot be upgraded, implement network isolation as a compensating control.
findings.description: The operating system identified from banners or Nessus output has passed its vendor support end-of-life date. The OS will not receive security patches for newly discovered vulnerabilities.
findings._x_remediation: Upgrade to a supported OS version. If the device cannot be upgraded, implement network isolation as a compensating control.

findings.title: Nuclei Template Match — CVE
findings.remediation_brief: Apply the vendor patch for the matched CVE. Verify remediation by re-running the nuclei scan.
findings.description: Nuclei matched a CVE-tagged template against the target. The response pattern confirms the service is exhibiting behaviour consistent with the disclosed vulnerability.
findings._x_remediation: Apply the vendor patch for the matched CVE. Verify remediation by re-running the nuclei scan.

findings.title: Nuclei Template Match — Misconfiguration
findings.remediation_brief: Correct the specific misconfiguration. Harden the service configuration against the ProjectDiscovery misconfiguration template library.
findings.description: Nuclei identified a security misconfiguration (exposed admin panel, default path, misconfigured CORS, insecure HTTP method, etc.).
findings._x_remediation: Correct the specific misconfiguration. Harden the service configuration against the ProjectDiscovery misconfiguration template library.

findings.title: Nuclei Template Match — Exposed Panel
findings.remediation_brief: Restrict access to administrative panels by IP allowlist, VPN, or disable public access entirely.
findings.description: Nuclei identified an exposed administrative or management panel accessible without prior authentication (e.g., Grafana, Jenkins, Kibana, phpMyAdmin, device management UI).
findings._x_remediation: Restrict access to administrative panels by IP allowlist, VPN, or disable public access entirely.

findings.title: SSL/TLS Certificate: Expired
findings.remediation_brief: Renew the certificate immediately and implement automated renewal (e.g., ACME/Let's Encrypt) to prevent future expiry.
findings.description: The server's TLS certificate has passed its expiry date, causing browser trust errors and indicating a breakdown in certificate lifecycle management.
findings._x_remediation: Renew the certificate immediately and implement automated renewal (e.g., ACME/Let's Encrypt) to prevent future expiry.

findings.title: SSL/TLS Certificate: Self-Signed
findings.remediation_brief: Replace self-signed certificates with certificates issued by a trusted CA; use ACME/Let's Encrypt for cost-free automation.
findings.description: The server presented a self-signed TLS certificate that is not anchored to a publicly trusted CA, preventing clients from verifying the server's identity and enabling trivial MITM attacks.
findings._x_remediation: Replace self-signed certificates with certificates issued by a trusted CA; use ACME/Let's Encrypt for cost-free automation.

findings.title: SSL/TLS — Protocol Version Below TLS 1.2
findings.remediation_brief: Disable TLS 1.0, TLS 1.1, and all SSL versions. Accept only TLS 1.2 and TLS 1.3.
findings.description: TLS 1.0 or TLS 1.1 is accepted. These protocol versions are deprecated by RFC 8996 and vulnerable to BEAST, POODLE, and RC4 downgrade attacks.
findings._x_remediation: Disable TLS 1.0, TLS 1.1, and all SSL versions. Accept only TLS 1.2 and TLS 1.3.

findings.title: SSL/TLS — Weak Cipher Suite Accepted
findings.remediation_brief: Configure the server to accept only AEAD cipher suites with forward secrecy (ECDHE-ECDSA-AES256-GCM-SHA384, TLS_CHACHA20_POLY1305_SHA256, etc.).
findings.description: The TLS server accepts cipher suites providing less than 128-bit security, null encryption, or anonymous key exchange.
findings._x_remediation: Configure the server to accept only AEAD cipher suites with forward secrecy (ECDHE-ECDSA-AES256-GCM-SHA384, TLS_CHACHA20_POLY1305_SHA256, etc.).

findings.title: SSL/TLS — CRIME / BEAST / LUCKY13 Vulnerability
findings.remediation_brief: Disable TLS compression. Migrate to TLS 1.2+ with AES-GCM-only cipher suites. Apply server-side BEAST mitigation (RC4 disabled, prefer AES-GCM).
findings.description: The TLS configuration is susceptible to a compression-based oracle (CRIME), cipher-block chaining attack (BEAST), or timing side-channel (LUCKY13). Specific vulnerability depends on testssl.sh output.
findings._x_remediation: Disable TLS compression. Migrate to TLS 1.2+ with AES-GCM-only cipher suites. Apply server-side BEAST mitigation (RC4 disabled, prefer AES-GCM).

findings.title: SSL/TLS — Missing HSTS Header
findings.remediation_brief: Add Strict-Transport-Security: max-age=31536000; includeSubDomains; preload to all HTTPS responses.
findings.description: The HTTPS service does not return a Strict-Transport-Security header. Clients may be susceptible to SSL stripping attacks.
findings._x_remediation: Add Strict-Transport-Security: max-age=31536000; includeSubDomains; preload to all HTTPS responses.

findings.title: SSL/TLS — Weak Certificate Signature Algorithm
findings.remediation_brief: Reissue the certificate using SHA-256 or SHA-384 as the signature algorithm.
findings.description: The TLS certificate is signed with a deprecated algorithm such as MD5 or SHA-1. These algorithms are vulnerable to collision attacks that could allow certificate forgery.
findings._x_remediation: Reissue the certificate using SHA-256 or SHA-384 as the signature algorithm.

findings.title: SSL/TLS — Certificate Hostname Mismatch
findings.remediation_brief: Reissue the certificate with the correct Subject Alternative Names matching all DNS names and IP addresses used to access the service.
findings.description: The Common Name or Subject Alternative Names in the TLS certificate do not match the host being connected to. Clients will receive a certificate warning or reject the connection.
findings._x_remediation: Reissue the certificate with the correct Subject Alternative Names matching all DNS names and IP addresses used to access the service.

findings.title: SSH Weak Configuration (Ciphers / Legacy Protocol / Credential Auth)
findings.remediation_brief: Harden sshd_config to disable SSHv1, restrict ciphers and MACs to strong algorithms, disable root login, disable password authentication, and require public-key authentication only.
findings.description: The SSH service is configured with one or more weaknesses including weak ciphers/MACs, SSHv1 support, permitted root login, or password-based authentication, increasing exposure to brute-force and protocol-level attacks.
findings._x_remediation: Harden sshd_config to disable SSHv1, restrict ciphers and MACs to strong algorithms, disable root login, disable password authentication, and require public-key authentication only.

findings.title: SSH Weak Configuration (Ciphers / Legacy Protocol / Credential Auth)
findings.remediation_brief: Harden sshd_config to disable SSHv1, restrict ciphers and MACs to strong algorithms, disable root login, disable password authentication, and require public-key authentication only.
findings.description: The SSH service is configured with one or more weaknesses including weak ciphers/MACs, SSHv1 support, permitted root login, or password-based authentication, increasing exposure to brute-force and protocol-level attacks.
findings._x_remediation: Harden sshd_config to disable SSHv1, restrict ciphers and MACs to strong algorithms, disable root login, disable password authentication, and require public-key authentication only.

findings.title: SSH Weak Configuration (Ciphers / Legacy Protocol / Credential Auth)
findings.remediation_brief: Harden sshd_config to disable SSHv1, restrict ciphers and MACs to strong algorithms, disable root login, disable password authentication, and require public-key authentication only.
findings.description: The SSH service is configured with one or more weaknesses including weak ciphers/MACs, SSHv1 support, permitted root login, or password-based authentication, increasing exposure to brute-force and protocol-level attacks.
findings._x_remediation: Harden sshd_config to disable SSHv1, restrict ciphers and MACs to strong algorithms, disable root login, disable password authentication, and require public-key authentication only.

findings.title: SSH Weak Configuration (Ciphers / Legacy Protocol / Credential Auth)
findings.remediation_brief: Harden sshd_config to disable SSHv1, restrict ciphers and MACs to strong algorithms, disable root login, disable password authentication, and require public-key authentication only.
findings.description: The SSH service is configured with one or more weaknesses including weak ciphers/MACs, SSHv1 support, permitted root login, or password-based authentication, increasing exposure to brute-force and protocol-level attacks.
findings._x_remediation: Harden sshd_config to disable SSHv1, restrict ciphers and MACs to strong algorithms, disable root login, disable password authentication, and require public-key authentication only.

findings.title: SSH Weak Configuration (Ciphers / Legacy Protocol / Credential Auth)
findings.remediation_brief: Harden sshd_config to disable SSHv1, restrict ciphers and MACs to strong algorithms, disable root login, disable password authentication, and require public-key authentication only.
findings.description: The SSH service is configured with one or more weaknesses including weak ciphers/MACs, SSHv1 support, permitted root login, or password-based authentication, increasing exposure to brute-force and protocol-level attacks.
findings._x_remediation: Harden sshd_config to disable SSHv1, restrict ciphers and MACs to strong algorithms, disable root login, disable password authentication, and require public-key authentication only.

findings.title: SMB Signing Disabled or Not Required
findings.remediation_brief: Enable and require SMB signing via Group Policy (RequireSecuritySignature=1) on all Windows systems to prevent NTLM relay attacks.
findings.description: SMB packet signing is not enforced on the server, allowing an attacker positioned between client and server to relay or tamper with SMB authentication and data.
findings._x_remediation: Enable and require SMB signing via Group Policy (RequireSecuritySignature=1) on all Windows systems to prevent NTLM relay attacks.

findings.title: SMB Share Accessible Without Authentication
findings.remediation_brief: Require authentication on all SMB shares, disable null-session and guest access, and enforce least-privilege ACLs on every share.
findings.description: One or more SMB shares are accessible without valid credentials, allowing unauthenticated users to read or write files and potentially enumerate domain information.
findings._x_remediation: Require authentication on all SMB shares, disable null-session and guest access, and enforce least-privilege ACLs on every share.

findings.title: SMB Share Accessible Without Authentication
findings.remediation_brief: Require authentication on all SMB shares, disable null-session and guest access, and enforce least-privilege ACLs on every share.
findings.description: One or more SMB shares are accessible without valid credentials, allowing unauthenticated users to read or write files and potentially enumerate domain information.
findings._x_remediation: Require authentication on all SMB shares, disable null-session and guest access, and enforce least-privilege ACLs on every share.

findings.title: Web — Default Credentials Accepted
findings.remediation_brief: Enforce mandatory credential change on first boot or provisioning. Implement account lockout after failed attempts.
findings.description: The web management interface accepted default manufacturer credentials. An attacker can gain full administrative access without any reconnaissance.
findings._x_remediation: Enforce mandatory credential change on first boot or provisioning. Implement account lockout after failed attempts.

findings.title: Directory Listing Enabled
findings.remediation_brief: Disable directory indexing (e.g., Options -Indexes in Apache; autoindex off in nginx) and ensure every directory contains an explicit index document.
findings.description: The web server is configured to display a browsable directory index, exposing file structure and potentially sensitive files to unauthenticated users.
findings._x_remediation: Disable directory indexing (e.g., Options -Indexes in Apache; autoindex off in nginx) and ensure every directory contains an explicit index document.

findings.title: Web — Missing Security Headers
findings.remediation_brief: Add all recommended security headers to HTTP responses. Review shcheck output for the specific missing headers.
findings.description: One or more recommended HTTP security headers are absent: Content-Security-Policy, X-Frame-Options, X-Content-Type-Options, Referrer-Policy, Permissions-Policy.
findings._x_remediation: Add all recommended security headers to HTTP responses. Review shcheck output for the specific missing headers.

findings.title: Header Data Leakage: Server
findings.remediation_brief: Remove or genericise the Server response header in the web server configuration (e.g., ServerTokens Prod in Apache; server_tokens off in nginx).
findings.description: The HTTP Server response header reveals the web server software name and version, reducing the attacker's reconnaissance effort needed to identify version-specific vulnerabilities.
findings._x_remediation: Remove or genericise the Server response header in the web server configuration (e.g., ServerTokens Prod in Apache; server_tokens off in nginx).

findings.title: Web — HTTP Exposed (No HTTPS Redirect)
findings.remediation_brief: Redirect all HTTP traffic to HTTPS. Enable HSTS to prevent downgrade attacks.
findings.description: The web application is accessible over plaintext HTTP and does not redirect to HTTPS. Credentials and session tokens transmitted over HTTP are observable to network attackers.
findings._x_remediation: Redirect all HTTP traffic to HTTPS. Enable HSTS to prevent downgrade attacks.

findings.title: Web — Insecure Cookie Attributes
findings.remediation_brief: Set Secure, HttpOnly, and SameSite=Strict (or Lax) attributes on all authentication and session cookies.
findings.description: Session or authentication cookies are missing the Secure, HttpOnly, or SameSite attributes. This exposes them to theft via JavaScript, plaintext transmission, or CSRF.
findings._x_remediation: Set Secure, HttpOnly, and SameSite=Strict (or Lax) attributes on all authentication and session cookies.

findings.title: Unencrypted Service: Telnet
findings.remediation_brief: Disable the Telnet daemon and replace it with SSH for all remote administration; block port 23 at the network perimeter.
findings.description: A Telnet service is accessible on the network, transmitting all data including authentication credentials in cleartext, enabling passive interception or active MITM attacks.
findings._x_remediation: Disable the Telnet daemon and replace it with SSH for all remote administration; block port 23 at the network perimeter.

findings.title: SNMP Default Community String Accepted
findings.remediation_brief: Change all SNMP community strings to random high-entropy values, restrict SNMP access by source IP, and migrate to SNMPv3 with authentication and encryption.
findings.description: The SNMP service accepts a well-known default community string (e.g., public/private), allowing unauthenticated read (and potentially write) access to device configuration data.
findings._x_remediation: Change all SNMP community strings to random high-entropy values, restrict SNMP access by source IP, and migrate to SNMPv3 with authentication and encryption.

findings.title: FTP Anonymous Login Permitted
findings.remediation_brief: Disable anonymous FTP in the server configuration; migrate file transfer to SFTP/FTPS and enforce authentication for all access.
findings.description: The FTP service accepts the anonymous username without credentials, potentially exposing hosted files or allowing unauthenticated file upload.
findings._x_remediation: Disable anonymous FTP in the server configuration; migrate file transfer to SFTP/FTPS and enforce authentication for all access.

findings.title: NFS World-Readable Export
findings.remediation_brief: Restrict NFS exports by client IP. Use root_squash and nosuid mount options. Disable NFS if not required.
findings.description: An NFS export is accessible to all hosts (wildcard * or 0.0.0.0/0 in /etc/exports). Any host on the network can mount and read the exported filesystem.
findings._x_remediation: Restrict NFS exports by client IP. Use root_squash and nosuid mount options. Disable NFS if not required.

findings.title: Deprecated or Weak Protocol in Use
findings.remediation_brief: Disable deprecated protocol services. Replace with modern, authenticated, encrypted equivalents.
findings.description: A deprecated or inherently weak network protocol was identified (e.g., RPC portmapper, rsh, rlogin, finger, X11 without auth, TFTP). These protocols provide no confidentiality or authentication.
findings._x_remediation: Disable deprecated protocol services. Replace with modern, authenticated, encrypted equivalents.

findings.title: mDNS / Bonjour Service Announcement
findings.remediation_brief: Disable mDNS service announcement on production devices if not required for operation. Apply network segmentation to prevent mDNS traffic crossing boundaries.
findings.description: The device is broadcasting mDNS (Multicast DNS / Bonjour / Avahi) service announcements. These expose device capabilities, hostname, model information, and available services to all hosts on the local segment.
findings._x_remediation: Disable mDNS service announcement on production devices if not required for operation. Apply network segmentation to prevent mDNS traffic crossing boundaries.

findings.title: RFID Card UID Captured
findings.remediation_brief: Implement mutual authentication (MIFARE DESFire EV2/EV3 with AES). Do not rely on UID alone.
findings.description: Proxmark3 successfully read the UID of an RFID credential within range of the device reader. Systems relying solely on UID for access control are vulnerable to cloning attacks.
findings._x_remediation: Implement mutual authentication (MIFARE DESFire EV2/EV3 with AES). Do not rely on UID alone.

findings.title: RFID Card Data Payload Read
findings.remediation_brief: Enable sector access conditions on MIFARE Classic cards. Migrate to DESFire with application-level encryption.
findings.description: The RFID card data blocks were successfully read without authentication. Sensitive data stored in card memory (employee ID, access level, personal data) may be exposed.
findings._x_remediation: Enable sector access conditions on MIFARE Classic cards. Migrate to DESFire with application-level encryption.

findings.title: RFID Replay Attack Successful
findings.remediation_brief: Replace credential infrastructure with challenge-response or rolling code systems. Audit physical access logs for anomalous events.
findings.description: A captured RFID credential was successfully replayed to the reader and accepted. No anti-replay protection is in place.
findings._x_remediation: Replace credential infrastructure with challenge-response or rolling code systems. Audit physical access logs for anomalous events.

findings.title: USB HID Keyboard Injection Accepted
findings.remediation_brief: Implement USB HID device allowlisting. Disable USB HID enumeration on production devices where not required.
findings.description: The device accepted keystroke injection from an emulated HID keyboard without any restriction or rate-limiting. A pre-programmed HID device can execute OS-level commands on device insertion.
findings._x_remediation: Implement USB HID device allowlisting. Disable USB HID enumeration on production devices where not required.

findings.title: USB Bash Bunny Payload Executed
findings.remediation_brief: Apply USB device policy and application whitelisting. Review autorun and HID handling in the OS.
findings.description: A Bash Bunny HID payload was executed by the device. The injected keystrokes were processed without restriction.
findings._x_remediation: Apply USB device policy and application whitelisting. Review autorun and HID handling in the OS.

findings.title: USB Abnormal Power Draw
findings.remediation_brief: Deploy USB power-only data-blockers on charging ports. Restrict USB host mode to known-good peripherals.
findings.description: Abnormal USB power characteristics were detected, potentially indicating a rogue charging cable or peripheral with embedded circuitry.
findings._x_remediation: Deploy USB power-only data-blockers on charging ports. Restrict USB host mode to known-good peripherals.

findings.title: HDMI CEC Command Injection Accepted
findings.remediation_brief: Disable CEC in firmware if not required. Apply command filtering to reject unauthorised CEC commands.
findings.description: Injected HDMI CEC commands were accepted and processed. An attacker with HDMI port access can issue remote control commands or exploit CEC stack vulnerabilities.
findings._x_remediation: Disable CEC in firmware if not required. Apply command filtering to reject unauthorised CEC commands.

findings.title: HDMI HDCP Not Enforced
findings.remediation_brief: Enable HDCP enforcement in device firmware.
findings.description: HDCP content protection is not enforced on the HDMI interface. Video/audio streams can be captured in cleartext.
findings._x_remediation: Enable HDCP enforcement in device firmware.

findings.title: HDMI DDC-CI Unauthorised Control
findings.remediation_brief: Disable DDC-CI in display firmware if remote monitor control is not required.
findings.description: DDC-CI commands accepted over HDMI allow monitor control (brightness, OSD) without physical interaction with the display.
findings._x_remediation: Disable DDC-CI in display firmware if remote monitor control is not required.

findings.title: EDID Information Disclosure
findings.remediation_brief: No action required if EDID is functioning normally. Consider custom EDID for high-security deployments.
findings.description: EDID data was successfully read, disclosing monitor model, serial number, manufacturer, and capabilities.
findings._x_remediation: No action required if EDID is functioning normally. Consider custom EDID for high-security deployments.

findings.title: Unauthenticated Serial Console
findings.remediation_brief: Password-protect the serial console in firmware. Disable UART console in production builds.
findings.description: A serial console (UART, RS-232) provided an interactive unauthenticated shell or bootloader prompt on connection.
findings._x_remediation: Password-protect the serial console in firmware. Disable UART console in production builds.

findings.title: Serial Console Baud Rate Identified
findings.remediation_brief: Review whether the console is accessible in production and restrict access if appropriate.
findings.description: The serial port baud rate was auto-detected. The presence and configuration of a serial console is documented.
findings._x_remediation: Review whether the console is accessible in production and restrict access if appropriate.

findings.title: CAN Bus Frame Captured
findings.remediation_brief: Ensure CAN bus access is physically restricted. Document observed frame IDs against expected device behaviour.
findings.description: CAN bus frames were captured from the device. Frame IDs and data payloads are documented for replay and fuzzing analysis.
findings._x_remediation: Ensure CAN bus access is physically restricted. Document observed frame IDs against expected device behaviour.

findings.title: CAN Bus Injected Frame Accepted
findings.remediation_brief: Implement a CAN firewall or gateway. Consider SecOC (ISO 21434) for safety-critical systems. Apply physical access controls to CAN connectors.
findings.description: An injected CAN frame was accepted and processed by the device. CAN has no built-in authentication; any node on the bus can transmit arbitrary messages.
findings._x_remediation: Implement a CAN firewall or gateway. Consider SecOC (ISO 21434) for safety-critical systems. Apply physical access controls to CAN connectors.

findings.title: Zigbee Traffic Captured
findings.remediation_brief: Enable Zigbee AES-128 network and link layer encryption (Zigbee 3.0). Rotate network keys periodically.
findings.description: Zigbee frames were captured from the device. Depending on the security profile, payloads may disclose network keys, sensor data, or command traffic.
findings._x_remediation: Enable Zigbee AES-128 network and link layer encryption (Zigbee 3.0). Rotate network keys periodically.

findings.title: Zigbee Flooding / Denial of Service
findings.remediation_brief: Implement rate-limiting on Zigbee join and message handling. Apply Zigbee channel scanning and jamming detection.
findings.description: The Zigbee network showed signs of packet flooding tolerance (or lack thereof). Injection of excessive frames caused degraded responsiveness.
findings._x_remediation: Implement rate-limiting on Zigbee join and message handling. Apply Zigbee channel scanning and jamming detection.

findings.title: ARP / DHCP Traffic Reveals Network Configuration
findings.remediation_brief: Informational — expected behaviour. Review whether observed network configuration aligns with intended design.
findings.description: Passive ARP or DHCP traffic captured during the ConfigDiscovery phase revealed network configuration details: default gateway, DNS servers, existing DHCP leases, and VLAN membership.
findings._x_remediation: Informational — expected behaviour. Review whether observed network configuration aligns with intended design.

findings.title: Plaintext Protocol in Boot Traffic
findings.remediation_brief: Replace plaintext boot-time protocols with TLS-protected equivalents. Use HTTPS for firmware update checks, SFTP for configuration retrieval.
findings.description: Traffic captured during device boot revealed cleartext protocols (Telnet, HTTP, FTP, TFTP) carrying potentially sensitive data including configuration pulls or update checks.
findings._x_remediation: Replace plaintext boot-time protocols with TLS-protected equivalents. Use HTTPS for firmware update checks, SFTP for configuration retrieval.

findings.title: Plaintext Protocol in Shutdown Traffic
findings.remediation_brief: Review and encrypt all shutdown-phase network communication.
findings.description: Traffic captured during device shutdown contained plaintext protocol traffic, potentially including final state synchronisation or credential exchange.
findings._x_remediation: Review and encrypt all shutdown-phase network communication.

findings.title: CAN Replay Attack
findings.remediation_brief: Implement SecOC (Secure Onboard Communication, ISO 21434 / AUTOSAR) for safety-critical CAN signals to add freshness counters and message authentication codes. Apply a CAN firewall or gateway to rate-limit and filter frames by ID and frequency. Physically restrict access to OBD-II ports and CAN bus connectors. Log and alert on unexpected frame repetition patterns.
findings.description: A previously captured CAN frame was successfully replayed and accepted as a legitimate message by one or more nodes on the bus. CAN provides no built-in authentication or sequence numbering, meaning any captured frame can be retransmitted at will to reproduce an action — such as unlocking a door, disabling a safety system, or triggering an actuator — without knowledge of the originating system. This class of attack is particularly dangerous in automotive and industrial control environments where CAN commands directly affect physical state.
findings._x_remediation: Implement SecOC (Secure Onboard Communication, ISO 21434 / AUTOSAR) for safety-critical CAN signals to add freshness counters and message authentication codes. Apply a CAN firewall or gateway to rate-limit and filter frames by ID and frequency. Physically restrict access to OBD-II ports and CAN bus connectors. Log and alert on unexpected frame repetition patterns.

findings.title: SSL/TLS Vulnerability: BEAST
findings.remediation_brief: Disable TLS 1.0 and TLS 1.1 on the server; accept only TLS 1.2 and TLS 1.3. Prefer AEAD cipher suites (AES-GCM, ChaCha20-Poly1305) over CBC modes. If TLS 1.0 must remain enabled for legacy clients, configure server-side mitigation by preferring RC4 (deprecated) or — better — use TLS_FALLBACK_SCSV and enforce cipher order.
findings.description: The TLS server accepts TLS 1.0 connections using CBC (Cipher Block Chaining) cipher suites, making it susceptible to the BEAST (Browser Exploit Against SSL/TLS) attack. BEAST exploits a chosen-plaintext vulnerability in the way TLS 1.0 initialises IV values for CBC, allowing an attacker with MITM position and the ability to inject chosen plaintext to perform a blockwise chosen-boundary attack and recover session cookies or other short secrets. While practical exploitation requires both network position and JavaScript injection into the victim's browser, the condition is easily avoided by disabling TLS 1.0.
findings._x_remediation: Disable TLS 1.0 and TLS 1.1 on the server; accept only TLS 1.2 and TLS 1.3. Prefer AEAD cipher suites (AES-GCM, ChaCha20-Poly1305) over CBC modes. If TLS 1.0 must remain enabled for legacy clients, configure server-side mitigation by preferring RC4 (deprecated) or — better — use TLS_FALLBACK_SCSV and enforce cipher order.

findings.title: SSL/TLS Vulnerability: LUCKY13
findings.remediation_brief: Migrate to TLS 1.3 or configure TLS 1.2 to use only AEAD cipher suites (AES-128-GCM, AES-256-GCM, CHACHA20-POLY1305), which do not use MAC-then-encrypt and are inherently immune to LUCKY13. Remove all CBC cipher suites from the server's cipher preference list.
findings.description: The TLS configuration accepts CBC cipher suites that are vulnerable to the LUCKY13 timing side-channel attack. LUCKY13 exploits a timing discrepancy in the MAC verification step of MAC-then-encrypt CBC cipher suites: the number of compression function calls differs based on where padding ends, allowing a statistical timing oracle to decrypt TLS records byte by byte. The attack requires many connections and precise timing measurements but has been demonstrated against real-world TLS stacks including OpenSSL.
findings._x_remediation: Migrate to TLS 1.3 or configure TLS 1.2 to use only AEAD cipher suites (AES-128-GCM, AES-256-GCM, CHACHA20-POLY1305), which do not use MAC-then-encrypt and are inherently immune to LUCKY13. Remove all CBC cipher suites from the server's cipher preference list.

findings.title: SSL/TLS Vulnerability: SWEET32
findings.remediation_brief: Disable all 3DES and Blowfish cipher suites from the server configuration. Ensure no cipher suite using DES, 3DES, IDEA, or Blowfish appears in the negotiated cipher list. Prefer 128-bit or 256-bit block ciphers (AES-GCM). Upgrade to TLS 1.3 where possible to eliminate legacy cipher negotiation entirely.
findings.description: The TLS server negotiates cipher suites using 64-bit block ciphers such as 3DES (Triple-DES) or Blowfish, making it vulnerable to the SWEET32 birthday attack. After approximately 2^32 blocks (~32 GB of data over a single TLS session), the birthday bound is reached and an attacker can exploit block collisions in CBC mode to recover plaintext. While 32 GB may seem large, long-lived TLS sessions — such as those in web applications with keep-alive or WebSocket connections — can reach this volume in hours.
findings._x_remediation: Disable all 3DES and Blowfish cipher suites from the server configuration. Ensure no cipher suite using DES, 3DES, IDEA, or Blowfish appears in the negotiated cipher list. Prefer 128-bit or 256-bit block ciphers (AES-GCM). Upgrade to TLS 1.3 where possible to eliminate legacy cipher negotiation entirely.

findings.title: SSL/TLS Certificate: Expiring Soon
findings.remediation_brief: Renew the certificate immediately to restore a full validity window. Implement automated certificate renewal using the ACME protocol (Let's Encrypt with certbot, acme.sh, or Caddy) to eliminate manual renewal dependency. Configure monitoring alerts when certificate expiry is within 30 and 14 days.
findings.description: The server's TLS certificate has a remaining validity of fewer than 30 days, placing it at imminent risk of expiry. Upon expiry, browser and client connections will be rejected with a certificate trust error, causing a service outage that appears indistinguishable from a site being down. In environments without automated certificate renewal, short expiry windows frequently result in user-facing downtime and may indicate a weak certificate lifecycle management process.
findings._x_remediation: Renew the certificate immediately to restore a full validity window. Implement automated certificate renewal using the ACME protocol (Let's Encrypt with certbot, acme.sh, or Caddy) to eliminate manual renewal dependency. Configure monitoring alerts when certificate expiry is within 30 and 14 days.

findings.title: SSL/TLS - Overly Long Certificate Expiry
findings.remediation_brief: Reissue the certificate with a validity period of 398 days or fewer. Transition to automated ACME-based 90-day renewal (Let's Encrypt) to align with current CA/B Forum best practices and reduce reliance on long-lived credentials.
findings.description: The TLS certificate has a validity period exceeding 398 days, in violation of the CA/Browser Forum baseline requirements adopted by all major browsers since September 2020. Certificates with excessively long lifetimes present elevated risk: compromised private keys or mis-issuance cannot be remediated without active revocation (which is poorly enforced by clients), and the certificate may outlive the cryptographic assumptions under which it was issued. Major browsers now hard-fail on certificates exceeding 398 days issued after the policy effective date.
findings._x_remediation: Reissue the certificate with a validity period of 398 days or fewer. Transition to automated ACME-based 90-day renewal (Let's Encrypt) to align with current CA/B Forum best practices and reduce reliance on long-lived credentials.

findings.title: FTP Bounce Attack Possible
findings.remediation_brief: Configure the FTP server to reject PORT commands where the specified IP address does not match the client's source address (disable FTP bounce in daemon configuration). Consider migrating from FTP to SFTP or FTPS. Apply firewall rules to restrict outbound connections from the FTP server to known-good destination addresses.
findings.description: The FTP server accepts the PORT command with arbitrary destination IP addresses, enabling FTP bounce attacks. In a bounce attack, an attacker directs the FTP server to open a data connection to a third-party host on any specified port, effectively using the FTP server as a TCP proxy to port-scan internal hosts, bypass egress filtering, or connect to services that would otherwise reject connections from the attacker's source address. This technique can also be used to transfer files to or from third-party machines without direct connectivity.
findings._x_remediation: Configure the FTP server to reject PORT commands where the specified IP address does not match the client's source address (disable FTP bounce in daemon configuration). Consider migrating from FTP to SFTP or FTPS. Apply firewall rules to restrict outbound connections from the FTP server to known-good destination addresses.

findings.title: NFS Export Points Enumerated — Potentially Unauthenticated Access
findings.remediation_brief: Restrict NFS exports to specific, authorised client IP addresses or subnets in /etc/exports; remove wildcard (*) or overly broad CIDR grants. Require Kerberos authentication (sec=krb5p) for sensitive exports. Disable the rpcbind/mountd showmount response if export enumeration by arbitrary clients is not required. Apply host-based and network firewall rules to limit NFS port access to authorised clients only.
findings.description: The NFS server responded to showmount queries, exposing a list of exported filesystem paths and their allowed client specifications. Depending on export configuration, an unauthenticated or low-privilege host on the network may be able to mount one or more of these exports and read or write files directly. Even read-only access to NFS exports can expose sensitive configuration files, SSH keys, or application data that facilitates further compromise.
findings._x_remediation: Restrict NFS exports to specific, authorised client IP addresses or subnets in /etc/exports; remove wildcard (*) or overly broad CIDR grants. Require Kerberos authentication (sec=krb5p) for sensitive exports. Disable the rpcbind/mountd showmount response if export enumeration by arbitrary clients is not required. Apply host-based and network firewall rules to limit NFS port access to authorised clients only.

findings.title: NFS Insecure Export Options
findings.remediation_brief: Audit /etc/exports and apply root_squash, all_squash, and nosuid to all exports. Remove no_root_squash unless there is a documented and approved use case. Prefer ro (read-only) where write access is not operationally required. Apply the most restrictive client specifier possible (explicit host or /32 CIDR).
findings.description: One or more NFS exports are configured with insecure options that increase the risk of unauthorised access or privilege escalation. Common insecure settings include no_root_squash (which allows root on the client to act as root on the server), rw on broad CIDR ranges, no_all_squash, or insecure (allowing connections from non-privileged ports). A client with rw and no_root_squash access can write arbitrary files — including SUID binaries or SSH authorised_keys entries — that enable full host compromise.
findings._x_remediation: Audit /etc/exports and apply root_squash, all_squash, and nosuid to all exports. Remove no_root_squash unless there is a documented and approved use case. Prefer ro (read-only) where write access is not operationally required. Apply the most restrictive client specifier possible (explicit host or /32 CIDR).

findings.title: Industrial/OT Protocol Exposure
findings.remediation_brief: Segment OT/ICS networks from corporate IT networks using firewalls or unidirectional security gateways (data diodes). Apply application-layer firewalls that understand industrial protocol specifics to whitelist expected command sets and source addresses. Disable unused protocol services on PLCs, RTUs, and HMIs. Monitor for anomalous command patterns.
findings.description: An industrial or operational technology (OT) protocol was detected on the network, including but not limited to Modbus/TCP (502), BACnet/IP (47808), EtherNet/IP (44818), DNP3, or IEC 60870-5-104. These protocols were designed for deterministic, low-latency communication in isolated control environments and provide no authentication, integrity protection, or confidentiality. Exposure of these services to untrusted network segments allows an attacker to read sensor data, issue arbitrary control commands, or disrupt physical processes.
findings._x_remediation: Segment OT/ICS networks from corporate IT networks using firewalls or unidirectional security gateways (data diodes). Apply application-layer firewalls that understand industrial protocol specifics to whitelist expected command sets and source addresses. Disable unused protocol services on PLCs, RTUs, and HMIs. Monitor for anomalous command patterns.

findings.title: Unencrypted Protocol Detected
findings.remediation_brief: Replace cleartext protocols with encrypted equivalents: SSH for remote administration, SFTP/FTPS for file transfer, HTTPS for web services, SNMPv3 for network management. If cleartext protocols cannot be immediately replaced, apply network segmentation and access control to limit exposure, and implement monitoring for credential interception.
findings.description: A network service communicating over a cleartext protocol was identified, including one or more of: FTP (21), Telnet (23), HTTP (80), TFTP (69), rsh (514), rlogin (513), rexec (512), or finger (79). Cleartext protocols transmit all data — including authentication credentials, session tokens, and sensitive application data — in a form readable by any attacker with network access, whether via passive interception on a shared segment or an active man-in-the-middle position.
findings._x_remediation: Replace cleartext protocols with encrypted equivalents: SSH for remote administration, SFTP/FTPS for file transfer, HTTPS for web services, SNMPv3 for network management. If cleartext protocols cannot be immediately replaced, apply network segmentation and access control to limit exposure, and implement monitoring for credential interception.

findings.title: Missing Secure Cookie Attribute: HttpOnly
findings.remediation_brief: Set the HttpOnly flag on all session, authentication, and sensitive cookies in the application or web server configuration. This flag prevents client-side scripts from accessing the cookie value while still allowing the browser to include it in HTTP requests.
findings.description: A session or sensitive cookie was identified without the HttpOnly attribute. Without this flag, the cookie value is accessible to JavaScript running in the page context, making it directly extractable by any cross-site scripting (XSS) vulnerability on the same domain. An attacker who finds a reflected or stored XSS flaw can trivially read the session cookie via document.cookie and hijack the authenticated session without needing to exploit the TLS layer.
findings._x_remediation: Set the HttpOnly flag on all session, authentication, and sensitive cookies in the application or web server configuration. This flag prevents client-side scripts from accessing the cookie value while still allowing the browser to include it in HTTP requests.

findings.title: Missing Secure Cookie Attribute: Secure
findings.remediation_brief: Set the Secure flag on all session, authentication, and sensitive cookies. Combined with a site-wide HTTPS redirect and HSTS, this ensures cookies are never transmitted over unencrypted channels.
findings.description: A session or sensitive cookie was identified without the Secure attribute. Without this flag, the browser will transmit the cookie over both HTTPS and plaintext HTTP connections. If the application supports or redirects through any HTTP endpoint — even briefly — the session cookie will be included in the cleartext request and is visible to network attackers. This condition is commonly exploited via SSL stripping attacks that downgrade HTTPS to HTTP before the Secure cookie check takes effect.
findings._x_remediation: Set the Secure flag on all session, authentication, and sensitive cookies. Combined with a site-wide HTTPS redirect and HSTS, this ensures cookies are never transmitted over unencrypted channels.

findings.title: Missing Secure Cookie Attribute: SameSite
findings.remediation_brief: Set SameSite=Strict for cookies used in purely same-origin contexts, or SameSite=Lax as a minimum to prevent cookie transmission in cross-origin subresource requests while allowing top-level navigations. Avoid SameSite=None unless the cookie must be shared in cross-site embedded contexts, in which case the Secure attribute is also mandatory.
findings.description: A session or sensitive cookie was identified without a SameSite attribute. Cookies without SameSite are sent by the browser in all cross-site requests, including those initiated by third-party web pages. This exposes the application to cross-site request forgery (CSRF) attacks, where an attacker's page silently makes authenticated requests to the target application using the victim's browser-stored session cookie, potentially triggering state-changing actions without user consent.
findings._x_remediation: Set SameSite=Strict for cookies used in purely same-origin contexts, or SameSite=Lax as a minimum to prevent cookie transmission in cross-origin subresource requests while allowing top-level navigations. Avoid SameSite=None unless the cookie must be shared in cross-site embedded contexts, in which case the Secure attribute is also mandatory.

findings.title: Misconfigured Secure Cookie Attribute: SameSite
findings.remediation_brief: If SameSite=None is required for cross-site embedding, the Secure attribute must also be present. Evaluate whether SameSite=Strict is appropriate; if so, upgrade from Lax to Strict. Review all state-changing endpoints to confirm they are protected by either SameSite=Strict or an additional CSRF token mechanism.
findings.description: A session or sensitive cookie was identified with the SameSite attribute set to an insecure value. Setting SameSite=None without also setting the Secure attribute causes the cookie to be rejected by modern browsers or sent over HTTP, while SameSite=Lax may be insufficient for applications requiring CSRF protection on all state-changing requests that can be triggered via cross-origin navigations. Misconfigured SameSite values indicate an incomplete implementation of the cookie security policy.
findings._x_remediation: If SameSite=None is required for cross-site embedding, the Secure attribute must also be present. Evaluate whether SameSite=Strict is appropriate; if so, upgrade from Lax to Strict. Review all state-changing endpoints to confirm they are protected by either SameSite=Strict or an additional CSRF token mechanism.

findings.title: Serial Port Allows Remote Access
findings.remediation_brief: Password-protect the serial console in device firmware and configure an inactivity timeout. Disable network bridging of serial interfaces unless strictly required; if required, protect access with authenticated VPN and firewall rules. In production firmware builds, disable UART console output and bootloader access entirely or require a hardware-present jumper to unlock.
findings.description: A serial console interface is accessible to an unauthenticated party via an exposed physical connector, a network-bridged serial server, or a serial-over-LAN (SOL) interface that is reachable from the assessment network. Remote serial access without authentication provides a root-level interactive session or bootloader prompt equivalent to physical presence at the device, bypassing all operating system access controls, disk encryption unlock prompts, and network-layer security.
findings._x_remediation: Password-protect the serial console in device firmware and configure an inactivity timeout. Disable network bridging of serial interfaces unless strictly required; if required, protect access with authenticated VPN and firewall rules. In production firmware builds, disable UART console output and bootloader access entirely or require a hardware-present jumper to unlock.

findings.title: HDMI CEC Bus Device Enumeration
findings.remediation_brief: No immediate action required if CEC is a necessary product feature. Review whether CEC device information could aid targeted attack chains and consider disabling CEC in firmware for devices where it serves no operational purpose.
findings.description: HDMI CEC bus enumeration was performed and active devices on the CEC bus were successfully identified without any authentication requirement. Discovered information includes logical and physical addresses, device type (TV, playback device, audio system), vendor OUI, and OSD name strings. While this finding is informational, it establishes the device topology and may support more targeted CEC command injection or denial-of-service attacks.
findings._x_remediation: No immediate action required if CEC is a necessary product feature. Review whether CEC device information could aid targeted attack chains and consider disabling CEC in firmware for devices where it serves no operational purpose.

findings.title: DDC/CI Display Control Channel Accessible
findings.remediation_brief: Disable DDC/CI in display firmware or OSD settings where remote monitor control is not operationally required. Apply application-layer access controls to software DDC/CI tools (e.g., ddcutil on Linux). For high-security deployments, use video switches that do not forward DDC/CI signals.
findings.description: The DDC/CI (Display Data Channel Command Interface) channel over HDMI or DisplayPort is accessible and accepts control commands without authentication. An attacker with physical or software access to the video source can issue DDC/CI commands to adjust brightness, contrast, input selection, colour profiles, and power state of the connected display, or to read monitor asset information (MCCS capabilities). In environments with strict physical security requirements, uncontrolled display manipulation represents a tangible risk.
findings._x_remediation: Disable DDC/CI in display firmware or OSD settings where remote monitor control is not operationally required. Apply application-layer access controls to software DDC/CI tools (e.g., ddcutil on Linux). For high-security deployments, use video switches that do not forward DDC/CI signals.

findings.title: Heartbleed (CVE-2014-0160) Vulnerability Detected
findings.remediation_brief: Upgrade OpenSSL to 1.0.1g or later (or 1.0.2 / 1.1.0+ for current branches). After patching, rotate all TLS private keys and certificates, revoke the old certificates, invalidate all active sessions, and reset any passwords that may have been in server memory during the exposure window. Verify remediation by re-running the Heartbleed check.
findings.description: The target is running a version of OpenSSL affected by CVE-2014-0160 (Heartbleed). The TLS heartbeat extension implementation in OpenSSL 1.0.1 through 1.0.1f fails to validate the length field in the heartbeat request, allowing an unauthenticated remote attacker to read up to 64 kilobytes of server memory per request without leaving a trace in standard access logs. Repeated requests allow an attacker to recover private TLS keys, session tokens, passwords, and other secrets from server memory over time.
findings._x_remediation: Upgrade OpenSSL to 1.0.1g or later (or 1.0.2 / 1.1.0+ for current branches). After patching, rotate all TLS private keys and certificates, revoke the old certificates, invalidate all active sessions, and reset any passwords that may have been in server memory during the exposure window. Verify remediation by re-running the Heartbleed check.

findings.title: Cleartext Credentials Captured
findings.remediation_brief: Immediately replace the protocol in use with an encrypted equivalent: HTTPS for web services, SSH for remote administration, SFTP/FTPS for file transfer, SMTPS or SMTP with enforced STARTTLS for mail. Rotate the captured credentials and investigate whether they are reused across other systems. Conduct a broader credential reuse assessment across the environment.
findings.description: A username and password pair was observed in plaintext within captured network traffic. The credentials were transmitted over an unencrypted protocol such as HTTP Basic Authentication, FTP, Telnet, SMTP AUTH (without STARTTLS), or SNMP v1/v2c, and are fully recoverable without any cryptographic attack. Captured credentials may be valid for the target service, other systems on the network, VPN access, or cloud console login if the user has reused them.
findings._x_remediation: Immediately replace the protocol in use with an encrypted equivalent: HTTPS for web services, SSH for remote administration, SFTP/FTPS for file transfer, SMTPS or SMTP with enforced STARTTLS for mail. Rotate the captured credentials and investigate whether they are reused across other systems. Conduct a broader credential reuse assessment across the environment.

findings.title: Hostname Identified
findings.remediation_brief: Ensure DNS naming conventions do not disclose sensitive infrastructure details. Restrict reverse-DNS resolution (PTR records) for internal hosts from being accessible to external resolvers. Disable NetBIOS name service (NBT-NS) where not required.
findings.description: A DNS hostname or NetBIOS name was resolved for a target IP address, providing a human-readable label for the host. Hostnames frequently encode information about the device's function, location, operating system, or network segment (e.g., dc01.corp.example.com, router-dmz-01, dev-sql-server). This information reduces the attacker's reconnaissance burden by allowing service correlation without port scanning and aids in target prioritisation during an assessment.
findings._x_remediation: Ensure DNS naming conventions do not disclose sensitive infrastructure details. Restrict reverse-DNS resolution (PTR records) for internal hosts from being accessible to external resolvers. Disable NetBIOS name service (NBT-NS) where not required.

findings.title: CEC Bus Devices Discoverable Without Authentication — {self.ctx.instance_key}
CEC Power State Exposed — Unauthorised Control Possible — {self.ctx.instance_key}
CEC Scan Complete — No Devices Responded — {self.ctx.instance_key}
Zigbee Device Susceptible to Flooding on {self.ctx.instance_key}
DB9 Port: No Active Protocol Detected —
Bluetooth Device Discovered
findings.remediation_brief: Reconcile every discovered radio against the authorised asset inventory; disable or shield Bluetooth interfaces that are not required.
findings.description: A Bluetooth (BR/EDR or BLE) device was detected during zero-knowledge scanning, along with its advertising data (address, address type, RSSI, name, service UUIDs, manufacturer data).
findings.impact: Confirms a live wireless attack surface and provides the address and advertised metadata needed to target every subsequent enumeration, pairing, and exploitation test.
findings._x_remediation: Reconcile every discovered radio against the authorised asset inventory; disable or shield Bluetooth interfaces that are not required.

findings.title: BLE GATT Service Enumerated
findings.remediation_brief: Where the GATT layout itself is sensitive, require an encrypted, bonded link before service discovery is permitted.
findings.description: The GATT server of a BLE device was enumerated without prior knowledge, revealing its services, characteristics, handles and properties (read/write/notify).
findings.impact: Discloses device function and defines the read/write/subscribe attack surface; unauthenticated enumeration is the first step toward characteristic abuse.
findings._x_remediation: Where the GATT layout itself is sensitive, require an encrypted, bonded link before service discovery is permitted.

findings.title: Classic Bluetooth SDP Service Enumerated
findings.remediation_brief: Disable unused BR/EDR profiles; restrict SDP exposure and require authentication for sensitive services.
findings.description: Classic Bluetooth (BR/EDR) SDP service records were enumerated (RFCOMM/L2CAP channels, profiles such as SPP/DUN/PAN).
findings.impact: Exposed SDP records widen the BR/EDR attack surface and can reveal legacy profiles (PAN/BNEP, DUN) with their own vulnerability history.
findings._x_remediation: Disable unused BR/EDR profiles; restrict SDP exposure and require authentication for sensitive services.

findings.title: Static or Public Bluetooth Address — Device Trackable
findings.remediation_brief: Enable LE Privacy with frequently-rotating Resolvable Private Addresses; distribute the IRK only to bonded peers.
findings.description: The device advertises with a Public or Static-Random Bluetooth address that does not rotate, rather than a rotating Resolvable Private Address (RPA).
findings.impact: A stable address lets any passive listener track and correlate a body-worn or clinical device (and by extension a patient) across time and location, and leaks the OUI/vendor.
findings._x_remediation: Enable LE Privacy with frequently-rotating Resolvable Private Addresses; distribute the IRK only to bonded peers.

findings.title: Sensitive Identifier Broadcast in Advertising Data
findings.remediation_brief: Remove serials and patient identifiers from the advertised device name and manufacturer data; expose per-unit IDs only via an authenticated, bonded GATT read; consider BT 5.4 Encrypted Advertising Data.
findings.description: The device broadcasts a serial number, patient identifier, or other per-unit token in its advertising name or manufacturer-specific data, in the clear.
findings.impact: A stable unique identifier in advertising defeats address privacy (the string becomes the tracking key) and discloses asset/patient information to any passive listener in range.
findings._x_remediation: Remove serials and patient identifiers from the advertised device name and manufacturer data; expose per-unit IDs only via an authenticated, bonded GATT read; consider BT 5.4 Encrypted Advertising Data.

findings.title: Just Works Pairing — No MITM Protection
findings.remediation_brief: Provision real IO capability and set the MITM bit (LESC Numeric Comparison or Passkey Entry); where no IO exists, use OOB pairing or an app-layer authenticated channel.
findings.description: The device negotiated Just Works pairing (SMP MITM-protection bit = 0, or an IO capability of NoInputNoOutput on either side), which provides no man-in-the-middle protection.
findings.impact: An active attacker in radio range can interpose during pairing and relay or modify the entire connection, because Just Works authenticates neither party.
findings._x_remediation: Provision real IO capability and set the MITM bit (LESC Numeric Comparison or Passkey Entry); where no IO exists, use OOB pairing or an app-layer authenticated channel.

findings.title: LE Legacy Pairing — Passively Decryptable
findings.remediation_brief: Require LE Secure Connections (ECDH P-256); reject SC=0 on any hardware that supports LESC (BLE 4.2+).
findings.description: The device negotiated LE Legacy pairing (SMP Secure Connections bit = 0). Legacy derives the session key from a weak Temporary Key (Just Works TK=0; Passkey Entry TK is a ~20-bit value).
findings.impact: A passively-sniffed pairing can be decrypted offline with crackle, recovering the Long-Term Key and all past and future bonded traffic for that pair.
findings._x_remediation: Require LE Secure Connections (ECDH P-256); reject SC=0 on any hardware that supports LESC (BLE 4.2+).

findings.title: Static or Reused BLE Passkey
findings.remediation_brief: Use a fresh, random, per-pairing passkey that is never hard-coded, printed, or reused across units; prefer Numeric Comparison or OOB where the UI allows.
findings.description: The device authenticates LE Secure Connections pairing with a static or reused 6-digit passkey — printed on the enclosure, embedded in firmware/manual, or identical across units — rather than a fresh random per-pairing value.
findings.impact: A hard-coded or shared passkey defeats the MITM protection of LESC Passkey Entry: anyone who can read the printed/documented value can complete an authenticated man-in-the-middle relay, reducing LESC to Just Works in practice.
findings._x_remediation: Use a fresh, random, per-pairing passkey that is never hard-coded, printed, or reused across units; prefer Numeric Comparison or OOB where the UI allows.

findings.title: Bluetooth Pairing Method Confusion
findings.remediation_brief: Pin the negotiated association model, present an unambiguous 'enter' vs 'compare' UI, and prefer OOB pairing.
findings.description: A man-in-the-middle can negotiate Numeric Comparison with one device and Passkey Entry with the other in the same ceremony; both use a 6-digit value, so the user reads the number one device shows and enters it into the other, completing a stable MITM even under LESC.
findings.impact: Defeats the highest LESC/MITM security level via the human factor (CERT VU#534195): the attacker holds a persistent interposed position while both devices report a successful pairing.
findings._x_remediation: Pin the negotiated association model, present an unambiguous 'enter' vs 'compare' UI, and prefer OOB pairing.

findings.title: Bluetooth Pairing Security Downgrade Accepted
findings.remediation_brief: Enforce a security floor (SC=1, MITM for sensitive functions, 16-byte key) and abort pairing on any weaker offer; re-verify the negotiated level before exposing sensitive GATT.
findings.description: The device completed pairing after a forced downgrade offer (Secure Connections cleared, IO capability set to NoInputNoOutput, and/or a reduced key size), instead of aborting.
findings.impact: A device that silently accepts SC=0 / Just Works / a short key when it can support stronger security is exploitable via an active downgrade man-in-the-middle in range.
findings._x_remediation: Enforce a security floor (SC=1, MITM for sensitive functions, 16-byte key) and abort pairing on any weaker offer; re-verify the negotiated level before exposing sensitive GATT.

findings.title: Short Bluetooth Encryption Key Negotiated
findings.remediation_brief: Enforce a 16-byte encryption key floor and abort pairing/connection on any shorter negotiated size.
findings.description: The device negotiated a maximum encryption key size below 16 bytes (BLE floor is 7). Short keys reduce brute-force cost and are the BLE analogue of the KNOB attack.
findings.impact: A negotiated key near the 7-byte floor allows an attacker to brute-force the session key and decrypt or inject traffic.
findings._x_remediation: Enforce a 16-byte encryption key floor and abort pairing/connection on any shorter negotiated size.

findings.title: Bluetooth ECDH Public Key Not Validated (CVE-2018-5383)
findings.remediation_brief: Update to post-2018 firmware/OS that mandates ECDH public-key on-curve validation.
findings.description: The pairing stack does not validate the peer's ECDH public key (Y-coordinate) during Secure Simple Pairing / LE Secure Connections, allowing a fixed-coordinate invalid-curve attack.
findings.impact: An in-range MITM present during pairing can force the shared secret into a small subgroup and recover the session key (~50% per attempt, retryable), fully compromising the session.
findings._x_remediation: Update to post-2018 firmware/OS that mandates ECDH public-key on-curve validation.

findings.title: KNOB — Bluetooth Encryption Key Entropy Downgrade (CVE-2019-9506)
findings.remediation_brief: Patch the host to enforce a minimum encryption key entropy (>=7 octets BR/EDR, 16 for LESC) and abort shorter negotiations.
findings.description: The BR/EDR encryption key-entropy negotiation (LMP) is not integrity-protected, letting a MITM force both devices to a 1-byte (8-bit) key.
findings.impact: The reduced-entropy key is brute-forced in real time, allowing an in-range attacker with no pairing or user interaction to decrypt and inject traffic on the link.
findings._x_remediation: Patch the host to enforce a minimum encryption key entropy (>=7 octets BR/EDR, 16 for LESC) and abort shorter negotiations.

findings.title: BLUFFS — Bluetooth Forward/Future Secrecy Weakness (CVE-2023-24023)
findings.remediation_brief: Reject low negotiated key lengths, adopt the SIG key-derivation fix, and operate in Secure Connections Only mode.
findings.description: Weaknesses in BR/EDR session-key derivation (Core Spec 4.2-5.4) permit unilateral, repeatable session-key derivation, breaking forward and future secrecy; combined with key-length downgrade it enables MITM and impersonation across sessions.
findings.impact: An in-range attacker can force reuse of a weak session key, decrypting captured traffic and impersonating a device across multiple sessions.
findings._x_remediation: Reject low negotiated key lengths, adopt the SIG key-derivation fix, and operate in Secure Connections Only mode.

findings.title: BIAS — Bluetooth Impersonation (CVE-2020-10135)
findings.remediation_brief: Enable Secure Connections Only mode and require mutual authentication in both directions.
findings.description: BR/EDR authentication does not mandate mutual authentication; via role-switch and SC-to-legacy downgrade an attacker impersonates a previously-paired master or slave without possessing the link key.
findings.impact: An attacker in range who knows the victim BD_ADDR can impersonate a trusted, previously-bonded device without any key material.
findings._x_remediation: Enable Secure Connections Only mode and require mutual authentication in both directions.

findings.title: BLURtooth — Cross-Transport Key Overwrite (CVE-2020-15802)
findings.remediation_brief: Apply BT 5.1 CTKD restrictions that forbid overwriting authenticated keys or downgrading key strength.
findings.description: In dual-mode devices supporting Cross-Transport Key Derivation (spec 4.2/5.0 before 5.1), an unauthenticated attacker in range can trigger CTKD to overwrite an authenticated bonding key with an unauthenticated or lower-entropy one.
findings.impact: The paired relationship can be silently weakened without user interaction, enabling MITM on a link the user believes is securely bonded.
findings._x_remediation: Apply BT 5.1 CTKD restrictions that forbid overwriting authenticated keys or downgrading key strength.

findings.title: BLESA — BLE Reconnection Spoofing (CVE-2020-9770)
findings.remediation_brief: Enforce mandatory authenticated and encrypted reconnection before accepting any data from a previously-bonded peer.
findings.description: BLE reconnection authentication is optional and often not enforced by the client, so a central accepts spoofed data from an impersonated peripheral without re-authentication after the first bonding.
findings.impact: An attacker spoofing the peripheral BD_ADDR can feed forged data (e.g. medical telemetry) to the consuming device on reconnect, with no user interaction.
findings._x_remediation: Enforce mandatory authenticated and encrypted reconnection before accepting any data from a previously-bonded peer.

findings.title: Unauthenticated GATT Characteristic Read
findings.remediation_brief: Set encryption/authentication-required permissions on sensitive characteristics; gate PHI behind LESC-authenticated bonding.
findings.description: One or more GATT characteristics returned data over an unpaired, unencrypted link (ATT Read Response with a value and no 0x05/0x0F/0x08 security error).
findings.impact: Any listener in range can read the exposed data with no credential; where it is PHI, telemetry, or configuration the confidentiality impact is severe.
findings._x_remediation: Set encryption/authentication-required permissions on sensitive characteristics; gate PHI behind LESC-authenticated bonding.

findings.title: Unauthenticated GATT Characteristic Write
findings.remediation_brief: Require an authenticated, encrypted, bonded link (LESC + MITM) for all writes; add application-layer authorization (signed / challenge-response commands) to control points and OTA.
findings.description: A GATT write to a device characteristic succeeded over an unpaired, unencrypted link (ATT Write Response with no security error).
findings.impact: Unauthenticated write access permits configuration change, actuation, factory reset, or firmware/OTA abuse with no credential — the highest-impact GATT finding, and safety-critical on a medical device.
findings._x_remediation: Require an authenticated, encrypted, bonded link (LESC + MITM) for all writes; add application-layer authorization (signed / challenge-response commands) to control points and OTA.

findings.title: Unauthenticated GATT Notification/Indication Stream
findings.remediation_brief: Require encryption on the CCCD and its source characteristic; do not start notifications before authenticated bonding.
findings.description: On an unpaired link the device granted a large ATT MTU and started notifications/indications after a CCCD write, streaming data without authentication.
findings.impact: Sensitive telemetry or PHI is exposed to any in-range listener without pairing; a large pre-auth MTU on a sensitive stream aggravates the leak.
findings._x_remediation: Require encryption on the CCCD and its source characteristic; do not start notifications before authenticated bonding.

findings.title: SweynTooth BLE SoC Vulnerability Surface
findings.remediation_brief: Update the BLE controller firmware/SDK to a patched release; where the SoC is end-of-life, apply architectural mitigations (restrict pairing, disable unused profiles, physical/RF controls).
findings.description: The device's BLE System-on-Chip belongs to a vendor/part with known SweynTooth firmware vulnerabilities in the Link Layer, L2CAP, SMP or ATT (crash, deadlock, or the Telink Zero-LTK Installation security bypass).
findings.impact: Depending on the SoC and SDK version, an in-range attacker can crash or deadlock the device (DoS, may require power-cycle) or, on affected Telink parts, install an all-zero LTK for arbitrary read/write — safety-relevant per FDA/CISA advisory ICS-ALERT-20-063-01.
findings._x_remediation: Update the BLE controller firmware/SDK to a patched release; where the SoC is end-of-life, apply architectural mitigations (restrict pairing, disable unused profiles, physical/RF controls).

findings.title: BrakTooth BR/EDR SoC Vulnerability Surface
findings.remediation_brief: Update the Bluetooth controller firmware to a patched release; for end-of-life SoCs, disable unused profiles, restrict connectability, and apply physical/RF controls.
findings.description: The device's BR/EDR System-on-Chip belongs to a vendor/part with known BrakTooth LMP/Baseband vulnerabilities (V1-V16), ranging from crashes and deadlocks to Espressif ESP32 arbitrary code execution.
findings.impact: An in-range attacker can crash, deadlock, or (on ESP32) execute code on the controller; several affected parts (e.g. TI CC2564C, Qualcomm CSR8811/8510) were 'no fix planned', leaving only architectural mitigation.
findings._x_remediation: Update the Bluetooth controller firmware to a patched release; for end-of-life SoCs, disable unused profiles, restrict connectability, and apply physical/RF controls.

findings.title: BleedingTooth Linux BlueZ Kernel Vulnerability Surface
findings.remediation_brief: Patch the kernel to 5.9+ (or vendor backport); set CONFIG_BT_HS=n to remove the A2MP path; rfkill unused radios.
findings.description: The Linux host behind the Bluetooth controller runs an unpatched BlueZ kernel (< 5.9), exposing the BleedingTooth family: BadKarma (L2CAP heap type-confusion), BadChoice (info leak), BadVibes (BLE ext-advertising heap overflow).
findings.impact: BadKarma chains to zero-click kernel remote code execution over BR/EDR from radio range; BadVibes needs only that the victim is scanning, with no BD_ADDR required.
findings._x_remediation: Patch the kernel to 5.9+ (or vendor backport); set CONFIG_BT_HS=n to remove the A2MP path; rfkill unused radios.

findings.title: BlueBorne Bluetooth Stack Vulnerability Surface
findings.remediation_brief: Apply the 2017-09+ vendor security patches; disable Bluetooth when unused.
findings.description: The host Bluetooth stack (Linux BlueZ, Android, Windows, or old iOS) predates the 2017 BlueBorne patches, exposing SDP/BNEP/L2CAP flaws that require only that Bluetooth is powered on.
findings.impact: An attacker in range can achieve remote code execution or MITM with no pairing and no user interaction; 'non-discoverable' is not a mitigation because the address is recoverable by sniffing.
findings._x_remediation: Apply the 2017-09+ vendor security patches; disable Bluetooth when unused.

findings.title: LE Secure Connections Confirmed (Passively Uncrackable)
findings.remediation_brief: Maintain LESC; additionally verify per-pairing random passkeys, no debug keys, and rejection of downgrade offers.
findings.description: The device completed LE Secure Connections pairing (ECDH P-256), confirmed on the wire by the Pairing Public Key / DHKey Check PDUs and/or a crackle result of 'LE Secure Connections'.
findings.impact: Positive assurance that the session key never crosses the air and the pairing is not passively crackable; residual risk shifts to implementation flaws (static passkey, debug keys, downgrade acceptance).
findings._x_remediation: Maintain LESC; additionally verify per-pairing random passkeys, no debug keys, and rejection of downgrade offers.

findings.title: BlueSmack / L2CAP Echo Denial of Service
findings.remediation_brief: Patch the stack for input-length validation; rate-limit/throttle L2CAP echo and connection requests; make the radio non-connectable when unused.
findings.description: The device degraded or reset under a bounded L2CAP echo / l2ping flood (BlueSmack), indicating it does not bound or rate-limit oversized echo requests.
findings.impact: An in-range attacker who knows the BD_ADDR can hang or reboot the device, denying service — critical for a safety or clinical device.
findings._x_remediation: Patch the stack for input-length validation; rate-limit/throttle L2CAP echo and connection requests; make the radio non-connectable when unused.

findings.title: Bluetooth Connection Exhaustion / l2ping Flood
findings.remediation_brief: Rate-limit inbound connection requests, cap concurrent connections, and recover gracefully; make the radio non-connectable when idle.
findings.description: Rapid L2CAP/ACL connection opens or a sustained l2ping flood exhausted the device's connection slots, causing it to refuse or reset connections.
findings.impact: An in-range attacker can deny service to legitimate centrals by consuming all available connection resources.
findings._x_remediation: Rate-limit inbound connection requests, cap concurrent connections, and recover gracefully; make the radio non-connectable when idle.

findings.title: Bluetooth Link-Layer Malformed-PDU Crash
findings.remediation_brief: Update controller firmware and host stack (PDU length/format validation, buffer bounding); disable unused profiles; rate-limit.
findings.description: The device crashed or deadlocked when sent a malformed Link-Layer / HCI PDU (the generic class covering SweynTooth/BrakTooth-style firmware defects and Android BlueFrag CVE-2020-0022).
findings.impact: A malformed advertising/connect/control PDU — often broadcast with no BD_ADDR required — crashes the target and can escalate to remote code execution on vulnerable stacks.
findings._x_remediation: Update controller firmware and host stack (PDU length/format validation, buffer bounding); disable unused profiles; rate-limit.

findings.title: Bluetooth Testing SKIPPED — No Adapter or Sniffer Available
findings.remediation_brief: Attach a BlueZ adapter for active GATT/pairing work, or flash a sniffer board via Quiver (Sniffle / nRF Sniffer / ButteRFly / Ubertooth) for passive capture, then re-run the module.
findings.description: No Bluetooth adapter or sniffer was selected/available for the instance, so Bluetooth/BLE testing was not performed.
findings.impact: The Bluetooth attack surface of the device was not assessed; the absence of findings does not indicate the interface is secure.
findings._x_remediation: Attach a BlueZ adapter for active GATT/pairing work, or flash a sniffer board via Quiver (Sniffle / nRF Sniffer / ButteRFly / Ubertooth) for passive capture, then re-run the module.
